It has been revealed that with 250+ client engagements across both agency and embedded in-house roles, Vitalii Khomenko has seen product teams from the inside in a way few designers have. Here he makes the case for a new kind of design workflow built for the AI era, and explains why the window to adapt is narrower than most founders think.

For the last decade, every startup conversation about speed eventually became a conversation about engineering. Hiring more developers, cutting scope, choosing a simpler stack, it was almost always a dev-side problem. Vitalii Khomenko, Principal Designer at Orizon Design and founder of Fluente LLC, argues that's no longer true. And he has a specific view on what teams should do instead.

It has been revealed that what makes Khomenko's perspective worth taking seriously isn't just seniority. It's the specific shape of his experience. Over a career spanning 250+ client engagements, he has worked both as an external specialist brought in to deliver and as an embedded designer who became the single connective thread between product, brand, and execution. That dual vantage point is rare. Most designers live on one side of that line. Khomenko has operated extensively on both, which gives him an unusually clear read on where friction actually originates inside product teams, and where it doesn't.

Industry observers note that his work spans early-stage startups finding their first visual language and established brands managing complex, multi-disciplinary design systems. Across that range, certain patterns repeat. And the pattern that started becoming impossible to ignore this year pointed him toward a conclusion that is reshaping how he thinks a modern design workflow should actually be structured.

Recent findings suggest that the bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved. And the workflow needs to move with it.

When shipping code was slow, the existing design workflow made sense. Multiple rounds of revision, user testing, iteration, all of that fit naturally into the window while engineering caught up. That window is now gone, and most design workflows were never updated to reflect it.

It has been revealed that "Founders are asking design teams to move at the same speed as an AI-assisted dev pipeline, and design doesn't compress the same way code does," Khomenko says. The result is a workflow that was built around a constraint that no longer exists, applied to a pipeline that has fundamentally changed around it.

In a recent development, the forced choice between polish and speed that product teams are now navigating isn't upcoming as a concept. What's new is how stark it has become, and how directly it traces back to a workflow problem rather than a people problem. "Because development is cheap and fast now, there's constant pressure to ship the next thing immediately," he explains. "But the products that actually retain users are still the ones where the details were considered carefully. Fewer revision rounds isn't a process improvement if it means shipping avoidable friction.".

Khomenko has watched this play out across enough teams, at enough stages, to be specific about where the existing workflow breaks down. The matter isn't design judgment. It's where that judgment sits in the process, and what format it's expected to produce at the end.

It has been revealed that to understand Khomenko's proposed fix, it helps to understand exactly where the current workflow stalls. For most product teams, the end of the design process looks like this: a designer produces polished, dev-ready screens inside Figma, and hands that file to engineering. Engineering then interprets those screens, translates the visual decisions into code, and builds from there.

That translation step, Figma file to working code, is where the pipeline now breaks down. AI-assisted engineering has made the building part dramatically faster. But the translation step hasn't changed. An engineer still has to read a Figma file, interpret spacing, extract assets, make judgment calls about component structure, and write the implementation from scratch. That process takes the same amount of time it always did.

Recent findings suggest that "The manual workflow inside Figma simply isn't keeping up with AI-boosted engineering," Khomenko claims. "The design handoff is quietly becoming the thing everyone is waiting on.".

The result is a pipeline where everything around the handoff has accelerated, and the handoff itself has become the single point of drag. Figma, in other words, was built for a world where engineering was the slow part. It wasn't designed to feed a pipeline where engineering moves at AI speed.

This is the core of what Khomenko is proposing, and it's a more significant structural shift than it might first appear.

In his workflow, Figma doesn't disappear. It moves. Rather than serving as both the exploration environment and the final delivery artifact, Figma becomes the visual exploration layer exclusively: the place where brand identity is established, layout logic is worked through, and design direction is validated. It remains the right tool for figuring out what something should look and feel like.

According to recent reports, but the final delivery, the artifact that actually goes to engineering, is code. Specifically, components built into prepared libraries that engineering can work from and scale directly, without any translation step in between.

Recent findings suggest that the difference in implementation speed is the point. When a designer delivers a coded component library rather than a Figma file, engineering doesn't need to interpret anything. The decisions are already expressed in the language they're building in. What previously required an engineer to read, interpret, and re-create from a visual reference now arrives ready to use. In a pipeline running on AI-assisted development, that difference compounds fast.

Recent findings suggest that "Figma is still the right place to explore what something should look and feel like," Khomenko notes. "But handing over a Figma file and asking engineering to implement it is now the slow path. Delivering in code is the fast path. That's the shift.".

According to recent reports, executing this workflow requires a different kind of designer, and Khomenko is direct about that. The UI/UX designer becoming a Design Engineer is, in his assessment, not a distant possibility. It is a matter of time, and the teams treating it as a future consideration rather than a present reality are the ones most likely to find themselves stuck at the handoff.

Recent findings suggest that but Khomenko is equally clear about what this shift doesn't mean. Delivering in code is one part of the role, not the whole of it. The full design cycle isn't going anywhere. Applying branding to imagery, producing animations, building marketing materials, these remain essential creative tasks that require a broad and varied toolkit well beyond code. "The designer of the near future isn't just generating code," he states. "They're moving across the full cycle, brand, motion, marketing, product, with design engineering as an crucial and growing part of that stack, not a replacement for it.".

It has been revealed that what changes is that code-ready delivery becomes a core expectation within that stack. The designer who can move fluidly from visual exploration in Figma to component delivery in code, while also carrying the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level consumers actually experience, is the profile that the upcoming workflow demands.

Khomenko is candid that no single version of this workflow has fully standardized yet. Every team is figuring it out differently. The tools are evolving, the handoff expectations are shifting, and the processes teams are building around all of it vary considerably. There is no off-the-shelf playbook.

Industry observers note that but this is precisely where his 250+ engagements become more than a credential. They're a dataset. Having watched enough teams, at enough stages, through enough cycles of tooling change, Khomenko can see through the noise of individual variation and identify what's directionally true even when the specifics are still in flux. "Each team's workflow is really custom at this stage," he indicates. "But some general patterns of how this is going to look in the near future are already visible.".

In a recent development, those patterns consistently point in the same direction: design judgment moving earlier, final delivery moving into code, and the designer's role expanding in technical range while staying broad in creative scope. The exact tools and sequences will keep shifting. The underlying logic of the workflow Khomenko is describing is already taking shape in the teams paying closest attention.

For founders and product leads, the workflow Khomenko is describing has direct implications for how teams are staffed, budgeted, and structured.

Front-load design judgment. The biggest leverage in the newly introduced workflow isn't faster execution, it's better problem definition before generation starts. Bring senior design thinking in earlier, when it can shape what gets built rather than polish what's already done.

In a recent development, separate exploration from delivery. Figma and the visual exploration phase serve a distinct purpose from the final delivery layer. Treat them as separate stages with separate expectations, rather than collapsing them into a single step expected to produce everything.

Shift the delivery expectation to code. Whether that means hiring for Design Engineer range, developing it internally, or restructuring handoffs, the end of the design pipeline needs to arrive in a form engineering can work from directly. The translation step is where time goes to die, and it's now the most avoidable part of the process.

Protect the full creative stack. Design engineering matters more than it ever has. It is not, however, the whole job. Teams that reduce design to code generation will lose the brand thinking, motion, and marketing creativity that differentiates products at the surface level owners actually experience.

Stay flexible. The workflow is still forming. Teams that build rigidity into their process now will find themselves redoing that work within a year. The teams getting this right are the ones building enough adaptability into their structures to absorb what's still coming.

Industry observers note that "The Figma handoff made sense when engineering was the slow part," Khomenko notes. "Engineering isn't the slow part anymore. Delivering in code isn't the future of design workflow. For the teams paying attention, it's already the present.".

#116560. Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1592 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware.
  • It has been revealed that locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it.
  • According to recent reports, the setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware. In a presentation shared at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), they found that because the hardware doesn’t automatically keep shared data updated across servers, necessary software overhead adds a 3-5µ (microsecond) delay per lock, each time servers access the same data. These minute delays effectively cancel out the benefits — a finding that comes as CXL memory pools are being proposed as a potential AI KV cache solution.

It has been revealed that locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it. This way, no two servers overwrite the same data at the same time. Within a given server, the CPU’s hardware handles that handoff in a fraction of a microsecond, but across these servers, software is in charge of enforcement.

According to recent reports, the setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box. The switch, which UT Arlington’s Peiran Du called “the only commercially available product we can use,” caps their setup at four servers. The catch is that there is no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations on “a real four-host CXL shared-memory system.”.

Recent findings suggest that this means no synced CPU caches and no hardware atomics between servers to build locks on, so software has to handle both. Writers publish their cached copy out to the pool and wait for it to finish, while readers throw out stale copies before reading, with the locks built from plain reads and writes, such as Lamport’s fast mutex. CXL 3.0 defines a hardware fix for the caches, called Back-Invalidate, but the researchers hadn’t received vendor confirmation that their platform supports it.

Aside from the lock acquisition penalty, which is “roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks,” there is a visibility cost: “one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs.” This is 0.94 µs, one way, compared to 1.91 µs for an RDMA write on their 400Gb/s InfiniBand, so the link isn’t the cause. A local compare-and-swap takes about 100 ns and, across servers, a lock’s median is 3.7 µs if uncontended, but 132 µs at the 95th percentile with several servers on one lock.

Recent findings suggest that the result: breadth-first search (BFS), a standard graph algorithm and a common benchmark, “gains nothing from adding a second host,” and was actually slower on four servers than on one, at 0.74s versus 0.55s. This was mostly not from the locks and barriers, which were only about 3.5% of its runtime, but due to the repeated flushing of shared state at every level.

On the other hand, throughput for a hash table — using independent buckets and per-host allocators — grew almost linearly when adding hosts. Triangle counting, another standard graph benchmark, also had a runtime reduction of more than half when scaling from one to four hosts.

Those costs matter, in part, because shared CXL pools are emerging as a fresh home for KV cache — an AI model’s stored record of a conversation’s state — once it outgrows GPU memory and a server’s own DRAM. The CXL Consortium’s SC26 session description says cloud providers and GPU makers “have highlighted CXL memory pooling as an effective approach for improving KV cache access.”.

According to recent reports, SK hynix, which makes CXL memory modules, highlighted a design that hands KV cache between GPU servers through a shared pool and claims 2.6x faster time to first token than standard RDMA setups. Its abstract also claims 3.0x lower P99 latency and 1.9x higher throughput. Micron, at SC26’s CXL Pavilion, showed its Abaco reference design of pooled CXL memory shared across rack servers and GPUs. It claimed 10x to 30x agentic AI gains, with famfs support for apps like Nvidia’s Dynamo.

According to recent reports, the need is real, even if efficiency gains have led to less cache needed per token. Vikram Sharma Mailthody of Nvidia Research mentioned at SC26’s Emerging Storage panel that his own analysis of open models on Hugging Face demonstrates KV per token falling “by 50% every twelve months” with “up to 78 times reduction so far,” giving the example that 128K context took “about 64 gigabytes” three years ago and now takes less than one. But context lengths are heading toward millions of tokens, and “the product of those two will keep increasing,” he said.

Industry observers note that agents also add to the demand. Earlier in the conference, a workshop talk by Argonne National Laboratory and RIT researchers, based on public AI serving traces, highlighted that a “session calls again ~2 min later, once its tools return: a 160 GiB recency cache keeps 1% of its context,” needing the GPU to recompute the rest, or about 99%. Recomputation is significantly slower and more demanding, and memory is needed to cache more.

That makes it a capacity problem more than a speed problem. “Memory capacity is becoming a dominant factor. Memory latencies have not been seen as a primary problem yet,” Mailthody noted. An agent’s context only has to survive a gap of a couple of minutes. It’s also ideal for any KV cache solution to be as inexpensive as possible, and given that a 128GB DIMM costs more than four times that of a 64GB DIMM last year. According to Intel’s Anil Godbole on SC26’s CXL panel, being able to add capacity past the DIMM slot limit — including reusing DDR4 — bolsters the case for CXL even further.

It doesn’t hurt that the KV cache handoff is write-once, read-many, which is the type of pattern that actually scaled in testing, although UT Arlington did not specifically test KV cache. Researchers behind OCEAN, a CXL emulator, backed this idea in the same paper session as UT Arlington, saying that software coherence is fine for read-heavy work, with hardware essential as writes climb. Its abstract reports that hardware coherence, at least in emulation, can give an 11x improvement at full coverage on Tigon database workloads.

Sources indicate that limitations still exist, which is why SK hynix, for one, is relying on “novel locking and coherence protocols” for its design. Hardware isn’t quite there yet, and Back-Invalidate might “be pretty costly,” Du noted, suggesting that both hardware and software coherence may be required.

Recent findings suggest that micron, which built prototype KV cache sharing into Nvidia’s Dynamo, noted two primary failure cases in a CXL Consortium presentation last month: where the writer’s data never reaches the pool, and where the reader never sees the updates. The first can be fixed by producers flushing before blocks are published, so unflushed blocks can never be found. The second is fixed with a consumer flush, that is, invalidation of their cached lines, before reading. These are the fixes and costs that UT Arlington was measuring.

According to recent reports, micron cut its flushing cost by flushing each slot only once, which works because KV cache is content-addressed — a slot in the pool that hasn’t changed stays coherent after its first flush. Micron’s presentation also notes that neither failure causes a crash. Instead, the read returns plausible-looking data, and the output is wrong in subtle ways, with the wrong tokens on some requests under cache pressure.

According to recent reports, working against CXL as a solution is the fact that the memory pooling only reaches within a rack today, Godbole mentioned; it doesn’t span a full data center. Marvell and Penguin Solutions, in collaboration and in addition to others like Lightelligence, have shown or revealed memory expansion and pooling over optical links, which could stretch pooling past a single rack. CXL is also “not the protocol to ferry such significant data,” Godbole added, as it’s built for smaller reads and writes, 64 bytes at a time, closer to how a CPU uses RAM. For bulk transfers, he said, RDMA is more efficient.

A research system called Beluga, in a paper published on arXiv a year ago, had KV cache in “a commercial CXL switch-based memory pool” with time to first token cut by 89.6% and throughput raised 7.35x compared with an RDMA-based setup once its cache was filled. This suggests some optimization could improve the usefulness of the technology, too.

CXL is clearly a hit or miss with how it is actually used being a main concern, with “a gap between the [CXL] spec and the implementation from different vendors,” according to UT Arlington’s Jia Rao. SK hynix’s second-generation CMM-DDR5, at 256GB and using CXL 3.2, has only been shown, and the device its KV cache design uses to select what to send is still what the firm’s Younghoon Min called a “research prototype.” These are early times, and the enterprise landscape is simultaneously changing promptly.

According to recent reports, on paper, shared CXL pools do fit the KV handoff idea, but until a commercial switch ships with confirmed coherence across servers, the best we have is KV cache numbers from vendor demos and research prototypes. Back-Invalidate should cut the software overhead UT Arlington measured, but Du expects it to add delays of its own; production systems would likely need a combination of hardware coherence and software approaches like Micron’s.

When Should You Remove NAT from an On-Prem Kubernetes Network?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In an on-premises Kubernetes environment, removing NAT can make the network simpler to inspect, reduce translation overhead, and let the data center route directly to workloads. But direct routing is not automatically the right choice.

Recent findings suggest that the decision depends on what the organization controls and what it needs from the network. A team that owns the physical fabric, has enough address space, and is comfortable operating BGP may benefit from making pod networks directly routable. A smaller environment, a team without control of the underlay, or a cluster that benefits from network abstraction may be better served by NAT or an overlay.

Kubernetes is also changing the ground under these decisions: kube-proxy is set to drop IPVS support starting with version 1.43, with nftables as the replacement. For on-prem teams already reviewing their service data path, it is a good moment to ask whether NAT still belongs in it.

So the useful question is not how to eliminate NAT, but when the operational benefits of doing so justify the additional routing responsibility.

Industry observers note that NAT solves a real problem. It allows an internal network to use its own address space without requiring the surrounding infrastructure to know how to reach every endpoint inside it. This is especially useful when you don’t control the underlying network.

According to recent reports, however, an on-premises data center is different. When you control both the Kubernetes cluster and the surrounding physical network, you can make Kubernetes networks directly routable.

In our case, removing NAT had practical and architectural benefits. It improved network performance, reduced CPU load on the nodes, and removed the risk of conntrack tables filling up on Kubernetes hosts. A directly routed L3 model also works well for traffic balancing when a node has two uplinks.

Recent findings suggest that this does not mean eliminating NAT from the data center entirely. NAT can remain at the boundary of the on-premises network, for example on hardware firewalls. Inside the data center, however, Kubernetes networks can be directly routable, allowing the physical network to reach workloads using the same routing mechanisms it already uses elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that in our implementation, BGP connects the Kubernetes network to the data center fabric: BIRD runs on the nodes and advertises pod CIDRs and selected service addresses, while kube-router manages Kubernetes networking. We described this implementation in more detail in our earlier article on building a routable on-prem.

Kubernetes cluster with BGP and ECMP. The vital point for this decision is not the particular stack, but the requirement it creates: the surrounding network must be able to accept and route Kubernetes prefixes safely. If the organization cannot or does not want to make the cluster part of its routing domain, keeping NAT or an overlay is usually the simpler choice.

Removing NAT alone does not make a network resilient. If every node still depends on one switch, one NIC, or one uplink, direct routing simply exposes the same physical single point of failure more clearly.

According to recent reports, the resilience benefit appears when the physical topology supports multiple independent paths. In our setup, nodes connect to independent data center switches and ECMP can use equivalent routes across those paths. If one path disappears, traffic can continue over the other.

That distinction matters when deciding whether direct routing is worth the effort. Organizations with redundant uplinks and switches can integrate Kubernetes into an already resilient routed fabric. If the underlay itself has no path redundancy, removing NAT should not be presented as a high-availability improvement: the physical failure domain still dominates the design.

Our stack is one example of how direct routing can be implemented, not a default recommendation for clusters that remove NAT. We chose kube-router because it supports a minimal installation as a binary and systemd service and covers the networking functions we need for this L3 design. BIRD handles route advertisements to the surrounding network.

It has been revealed that other environments may reasonably choose Calico for conventional L3 routing or Cilium when an eBPF-based dataplane and its additional capabilities are useful. The choice of CNI and routing daemon is secondary to the architectural decision: first decide whether exposing Kubernetes prefixes to the physical network makes operational sense, then choose the implementation that fits the team’s requirements.

In a recent development, A directly routed Kubernetes network is not automatically better than an overlay or NAT-based architecture. Each model solves a different operational problem.

According to recent reports, NAT is a reasonable choice when the cluster needs to remain isolated from the surrounding address plan, when pod addresses cannot be routed through the data center, or when the infrastructure team does not control the upstream network. It also keeps Kubernetes-specific prefixes out of the physical routing domain, which can be valuable for smaller environments where direct visibility into every pod is not important.

In a recent development, an overlay is useful when portability and abstraction matter more than exposing the physical packet path. It lets Kubernetes networking remain largely independent of the underlay and can simplify deployment across heterogeneous infrastructure. The tradeoff is another layer to inspect during troubleshooting and, depending on the implementation, encapsulation overhead.

Direct routing makes the most sense when the organization owns the physical network, has address space available for pod CIDRs, and has operators comfortable with BGP and route filtering. It becomes more attractive when preserving source addresses, using standard network troubleshooting tools, predictable performance, or integrating the cluster with redundant data center paths are important. At a larger scale, those operational benefits can justify the extra coordination between Kubernetes and network teams.

It has been revealed that the broader lesson is not that every Kubernetes cluster needs BGP or that NAT should disappear everywhere. It is that Kubernetes has matured enough that we should stop automatically treating its network as a black box.

As more production and AI workloads move onto Kubernetes, network architecture becomes part of application reliability. In an on-premises data center, BGP and ECMP give us the option to use the resilience already available in the physical network rather than building another isolated networking layer on top of it.

It has been revealed that sometimes the best way to make Kubernetes networking more robust is not to add another abstraction, but to remove one. But only when the surrounding infrastructure and the team operating it are ready to take responsibility for the routing that abstraction previously hid.

It has been revealed that if most of those answers are yes, direct routing is worth serious consideration. If not, NAT or an overlay may be the more resilient operational choice—not because it is technically more advanced, but because it better matches the environment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after noticing that his Elecbrakes remote had automatically paired to a stranger's trailer, Patrick Forck's cybersecurity spider senses tingled.
  • The story goes that Forck was a contented user of the Elecbrakes solution for the trailer towing fraternity.
  • It has been revealed that forck and McCarthy's first step on the road to a solution was to use Claude to do the heavy lifting on the reverse engineering of the Elecbrakes Android app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after noticing that his Elecbrakes remote had automatically paired to a stranger's trailer, Patrick Forck's cybersecurity spider senses tingled. Any feelings of foreboding were warranted, as it was discovered that a critical Bluetooth security flaw meant anyone could connect to an Elecbrakes controller "without pairing, authentication, a PIN, or any approval." Over the following 10 months, Forck and his Element Digital colleague Jeremy McCarthy would fully identify the vulnerabilities, make responsible disclosures to the vendor, work on fix verification, and more.

The story goes that Forck was a contented user of the Elecbrakes solution for the trailer towing fraternity. The firm's systems are claimed to be easy DIY plug-and-play controllers for enhanced braking response – crucial for trailer towing, especially with larger and heavier loads. The core functionality wasn't a problem, but Forck was alarmed when driving down the highway one day and noticed that his Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else’s trailer. "It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea," explained our tech-savvy protagonist. It wasn't long before he thought, "If a device I don’t own will happily talk to my in-car remote driving past with zero friction… what exactly is stopping my phone or any other Bluetooth device from talking back?" Clearly, Elecbrakes ' ease of use was unintentionally too powerful.

It has been revealed that forck and McCarthy's first step on the road to a solution was to use Claude to do the heavy lifting on the reverse engineering of the Elecbrakes Android app. McCarthy built a Web Bluetooth research tool that runs in Chrome, again using Claude. Then Forck tested the newly built tool with his car and trailer on some gravel roads on his family estate. It was confirmed that any attacker could connect via Bluetooth from nearby without Bluetooth pairing or authentication. Moreover, they could send simple commands to the trailer, apply braking at any force level, and receive confirmation that the brake had engaged.

As per the blog post documenting the finding and fixing of these vulnerabilities, the danger of a security flaw which "outputs torque to a wheel on a public road," is difficult to overstate. Especially when the attack surface and opportunity are open to “anyone within Bluetooth range.”.

Recent findings suggest that with the bulk of research complete, the Element Digital colleagues disclosed the information to Elecbrakes in May 2026. They were pleased with the small firm's responsiveness and openness. By July, firmware updates to patch the EB2 and VM1 models currently on the market were released.

An older Elecbrakes controller called the ELBC 2000 was discovered to have the same Bluetooth security flaws. The vulnerability of this model, which hasn't been sold for a number of years, has now been confirmed by the maker. Nevertheless, some folks will be using it on public roads. Elecbrakes has advised owners to keep an eye on firmware revision notices for an impending fix.

#116545. Samsung just introduced a gaming monitor with a refresh rate higher than its price — dual-mode Odyssey G60H offers 1,100 Hz in HD

📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Samsung just introduced a gaming monitor with a refresh rate higher than its price — dual-mode Odyssey G60H offers 1,100 Hz in HD

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that samsung's display business has produced some incredible screens, often with groundbreaking features.
  • It has been revealed that if you look at the specifications, you'll see Samsung describe it as a 600Hz gaming monitor.
  • Aside from the resolution and refresh rate specs, this is actually a fairly standard IPS LCD gaming monitor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that samsung's display business has produced some incredible screens, often with groundbreaking features. We have one such example released today: the Samsung Odyssey G60H (LS27HG602ENXZA), a 27" Fast IPS LCD gaming monitor whose standout feature is that it can refresh up to 1,100 times per second. That is 0.91 milliseconds per frame. This exotic screen isn't cheap, but if you're expecting a price to match the max refresh, be surprised, as you can snag it on Amazon for $894.

It has been revealed that if you look at the specifications, you'll see Samsung describe it as a 600Hz gaming monitor. There's no overclocking shenanigans here; this is a "Dual Mode" monitor, meaning that in its native QHD resolution (2560×1440), it supports an already scorching 600Hz refresh rate. You have to slash the resolution by 75% to get that 1100Hz figure, down to just 1280×720, or "HD". Given that this is exactly 1/4 the resolution of QHD, Samsung has hopefully implemented some pretty fancy integer upscaling.

Aside from the resolution and refresh rate specs, this is actually a fairly standard IPS LCD gaming monitor. That's not a knock; it's perfectly fine, with a typical brightness of 400 cd/m², claimed 99% sRGB coverage, rated 1000:1 native contrast, and some measure of HDR10 support—although given the lack of local dimming and the modest brightness, it's hard to call this an HDR display. Naturally, it supports FreeSync Premium and is G-Sync Compatible, and while Samsung doesn't share the VRR ranges, it does say that you can't hit the peak 1,100 refresh rate with FreeSync enabled.

The firm does say that the G60H is the first to include "Odyssey Clear Motion," a feature that it notes "reduces motion blur to help players see fast-moving action more clearly during critical moments in gameplay." It's not completely clear what this feature actually is, but Samsung says that "through the optimised blur reduction algorithm, the Odyssey G6 keeps fast-changing scenes clear and crisp.".

In a recent development, samsung notes that it intends to bring the technology to more gaming monitor models, which sounds interesting. Black frame insertion (BFI) and backlight strobing are the two most common methods of motion blur reduction, but Samsung has sold monitors with strobing for over ten years; it would be odd to reintroduce it as a upcoming feature now.

There's an interesting question hanging over this feature: at 1,100Hz, does a monitor even need dedicated motion blur reduction? Blur Busters has long discussed 1,000Hz as something of a milestone for sample-and-hold displays, arguing that sufficiently high refresh rates can approach the motion clarity of a CRT without requiring backlight strobing.

1,000Hz isn't some magical threshold where motion blur disappears entirely, though. That site's own calculations still predict about one pixel of motion blur for every 1,000 pixels per second of movement at 1ms persistence, and that's assuming instantaneous pixel transitions (like an OLED). At 1,100Hz, that drops to about 0.91 pixels, which is certainly impressive, but not quite zero. The monitor's actual pixel response times also factor into the equation, of course, and Samsung's claimed 1ms GtG response time is actually a measured range of 1.00 to 1.99ms, rounded down to a whole number. I'd be shocked if the real pixel response times weren't more like 3-5ms in the worst case.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Whatever the case with the motion blur feature, in terms of connectivity, the Odyssey G6 can accept video through DisplayPort 2.1 or HDMI 2.1. It has two full-sized HDMI ports, and it also has a USB Type-B connector to pass through its pair of USB Type-A ports to the host machine. Curiously, no USB Type-C connectivity is to be found anywhere, which is unusual on a monitor of this price class, but given that this is clearly aimed at desktop gamers who have the hardware to push games to these kinds of frame rates (at least, with frame generation), it's a sensible omission to be sure, as is the elision of integrated speakers. There is a headphone jack to pass-through HDMI audio, though.

The other crucial characteristics you might like to know are that the Odyssey G6 (G60)'s included stand supports tilt, swivel, pivot, and height adjustments; it supports 100×100 VESA mounting, and that it uses an external AC adaptor, not an internal power supply, which is bad for convenience but good for repairability.

In a recent development, while the image quality is not going to blow you away if you're accustomed to OLEDs, having seen a 540-Hz display in person and been gobsmacked by it, 1,100 Hz sounds absolutely tantalizing. Admittedly, 1280x720 is a low resolution, but we used to play 240p console games on titanic projection TVs. Hardcore competitive gamers don't need high resolutions, so every cut to input lag helps.

Japanese streamer Haigure Tamao has managed to escape GTA 6’s supposedly impossible six-star Wanted level by using an elaborate Easter egg that transports players into the original Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.

After ditching the sixth Wanted star in GTA 5, Rockstar brought it back for GTA 6, but with a major twist.

While players can normally escape the police by changing their appearance, switching vehicles or hiding, reaching six stars is supposed to leave them with just two options: death or arrest.

Even trying to escape in a jet just results in missiles being released at you.

GTA VI çıktığı günden beri 6 Yıldız aranma seviyesinden kurtulan kimse olmadı.Eğer jete binersenizFüze atan 5 jet sizi kovalarEğer arabayla kaçarsanız5 taaruz Helikopteri sizi kovalarEğer bir eve saklanırsanız,ordu eve tankla gelir…☠️ pic.twitter.com/5ICWx6QuRv.

However, one player has discovered a clever way to cheat the system with some help from Rockstar’s 2002 classic.

In a video uploaded to YouTube, Tamao, using his VTuber avatar, explained that he wanted to test whether entering the portal featured in GTA 6’s Tommy Vercetti Easter egg would erase his Wanted level.

The secret requires players to solve a puzzle spanning 12 electrical substations across Leonida before accessing a portal inside the Turtle Head Power Station between 7 PM and 6 AM in-game.

Entering it transports Jason to a recreation of the original Malibu Club, complete with PS2-era graphics and an appearance from returning character Kent Paul.

世界初？GTA6で手配度6から逃げきることに成功しました pic.twitter.com/0g7pSPJ6UU.

After struggling to survive his initial attempt, the streamer completed an entirely different secret involving the president’s hidden bunkers to get his hands on a powerful tank.

With his newly acquired vehicle, the YouTuber wreaked havoc near the power station, eventually reaching six stars with just minutes to spare before the portal closed.

Sources indicate that upon entering the retro Vice City, his Wanted level immediately disappeared. However, the biggest question was whether it would return once he was transported back to modern-day Leonida.

“The moment of truth,” Tamao said, translated from Japanese.

Much to his delight, the six stars were nowhere to be seen.

“I finally did it! I went from a Wanted level of six to zero!” he celebrated.

Whether Rockstar intended for players to use the Easter egg this way remains unclear, but the discovery adds yet another layer to one of GTA 6’s most elaborate secrets.

Players have already uncovered some incredible surprises since launch, including Dexter Morgan’s apartment and boat and a glitch that enables first-person gameplay.

As it turns out, the best way to escape Vice City’s police might be to leave their generation of GTA altogether.

Recent findings suggest that the Nvidia board has reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO just 11 days after he resigned, a move that, although it had strong support from both employees and supporters, had surprised many. While the company’s board of directors voted unanimously to bring the founder back, it seems that this decision was pushed along by pressure from Washington. According to CNN, President Donald Trump, alongside Vice President JD Vance and several members of his cabinet, spent the weekend talking to industry insiders, investors, and even to the board itself to get Jensen back as the chief of Nvidia.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump mentioned in an interview with CNBC. “I think we have one of our great stars back in play.” Nvidia’s stock price took a beating when Jensen Huang admitted to the affairs, and his future at the company was in question. It went from bad to worse when he finally resigned on November 12, with the rest of the market following. This has brought concerns that Jensen’s downfall would drag Nvidia and the economy with him, which could potentially turn into a catastrophe as the AI bubble pops.

The President said that bringing Jensen back as the CEO of Nvidia would be the only solution to this conundrum. True enough, Nvidia stock prices shot up to around $165 after Jensen’s reinstatement — a more than 25% rally from its previous close of around $130. “It’s a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it’s taking the whole market,” the president added. “It could be that there’s never been anything like it.”.

Despite the seemingly positive impact of Jensen Huang’s return to the company, Trump’s decision to intervene in the inner workings of a private institution has raised apprehension among politicians, even those from his own party. The biggest concerns raised include the Nvidia CEO’s involvement in national security challenges, including his affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia chips that have been allegedly smuggled despite the government’s export controls, and the fact that the President assured the Nvidia board that his administration does not believe that Jensen is a threat to national security and that he also was not facing any criminal charges, despite ongoing investigations. People also raised questions about the White House’s influence on the board of directors of a private company, something that was characterized as “an unprecedented campaign.”.

Trump’s push for Jensen Huang’s return at Nvidia is inherently risky, with the president himself saying that he had consulted Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton about it. He said that they’ve been studying the issue for quite some time and that they had found nothing wrong, especially as Trump said that he can’t have anyone indicted after making the recommendation.

Influencer Christie Miller has announced her own death at the age of 60 in a pre-recorded video following a four-year battle with breast cancer.

Miller was diagnosed with stage 4 HER2-positive breast cancer in June 2022 and amassed over 50,000 followers on Instagram by documenting her experiences with the disease and encouraging others to find joy in their lives.

The influencer also suffered a devastating personal loss in June 2025 when her husband of 36 years, Mark Miller, died from pancreatic cancer.

On November 23, a video was uploaded to Miller’s Instagram account in which she revealed that she had died and expressed her happiness at being reunited with her late husband.

“If you are seeing this video, it means that I am dead,” she said, before a montage of photos of the couple played alongside Peaches & Herb’s song ‘Reunited.’.

A post shared by Christie Miller | Chief Joy Officer (@iamchristiemiller).

Despite the circumstances surrounding the video, Miller was smiling and dressed in a colorful costume as she reflected on her life.

Recent findings suggest that “Don’t be sad because it’s over, be happy because it happened,” she said, quoting Dr. Seuss.

She encouraged her followers to allow themselves to grieve while also cherishing the memories they had made together.

“I have lived this beautiful life with no regrets,” she remarked.

In the days leading up to her death, Miller continued to share videos of herself enjoying some of her favorite activities.

Miller visited the beach with her dog on November 15 and spent what she believed would be her final week enjoying some of her favorite childhood foods, including a root beer float.

A post shared by Christie Miller | Chief Joy Officer (@iamchristiemiller).

Miller ended her farewell video by encouraging viewers not to let fear or other people’s opinions dictate how they live.

“Go out there and find joy every single day,” she noted.

The caption accompanying the video confirmed that Miller died peacefully on the morning of November 23, surrounded by love.

Sources indicate that miller is one of several influencers to have recorded their own death announcements. In August 2026, TikToker Andreethegirl shared a final message with her followers after dying from cancer at 39.

It has been revealed that picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

Shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that proposal. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

Whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide reveals how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

It has been revealed that wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and intends auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

According to recent reports, medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the company claims you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Google files patent for AI-generated TV channel that uses your face and voice for shows

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google has filed a patent application for a personalized television channel that uses artificial intelligence to generate shows starring the person watching.
  • Streaming platforms such as YouTube and Netflix already use viewing habits to recommend content, while companies have also started experimenting with broadcasting entirely AI-generated entertainment.
  • Google’s patent application, titled “Creating a Channel of Video Experiences Tailored to a User,” was originally filed on May 13, 2025, before being published by the US Patent and Trademark Office on November 19, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has filed a patent application for a personalized television channel that uses artificial intelligence to generate shows starring the person watching.

Streaming platforms such as YouTube and Netflix already use viewing habits to recommend content, while companies have also started experimenting with broadcasting entirely AI-generated entertainment.

Google’s patent application, titled “Creating a Channel of Video Experiences Tailored to a User,” was originally filed on May 13, 2025, before being published by the US Patent and Trademark Office on November 19, 2026.

First spotted by Patentlyze, the application describes a feature called “My Channel” that would appear within a television app and offer a selection of videos created specifically for individual viewers.

The system would use information including a person’s viewing history, location, language settings, and demographic data to determine what kinds of reveals they might enjoy.

Google could then use photographs to create a digital avatar of the viewer and replicate their voice, allowing them to star in everything from romantic comedies to science fiction adventures.

In a recent development, one example included in the filing describes how the system could generate a video starring someone who had recently watched cricket highlights. The viewer could appear in the stands during the Cricket World Cup or interact with one of their favorite players.

Recent findings suggest that users wouldn’t necessarily have to request fresh content, either. The application outlines a scheduling system that could automatically generate videos on a weekly, monthly, or yearly basis. It also describes a mechanism for inserting advertisements into the generated content.

Google now lets anyone make & use their own Android apps using AI.

Newly introduced Microsoft patent could use AI to alter speech and lip movements in real time.

YouTube tests prompt-based custom feeds that let you control your homepage.

According to recent reports, however, Google has not declared plans to launch the feature. According to Patentlyze, a patent examiner has issued a final rejection of the application, although the company can still amend its claims or appeal the decision.

The filing comes as AI-generated programming has already made its way onto streaming platforms, with Roku introducing a television channel dedicated to broadcasting AI-generated content around the clock.

Bambu Lab P3C Review: A more affordable tool changer

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Bambu Lab P3C is the lower-cost little brother of the H3C.
  • Works with multiple materials and nozzle sizes in the same print.
  • In a recent development, why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Bambu Lab P3C is the lower-cost little brother of the H3C. It has the same type of tools and outstanding TPU printing process as its larger sibling, but drops the heated chamber, filament dryer, and automatic filament loading. If you want an upgradable tool changer on a more manageable budget, the P3C is a great place to start.

Works with multiple materials and nozzle sizes in the same print.

Works with almost all spool types.

Changing tools is a pain, literally.

In a recent development, why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Bambu Lab didn’t even tease the arrival of the new P3C, a smaller, more budget-friendly version of the H3C, which retails at roughly half the price. In fact, this post might be the first time you’ve heard more than just a rumor about the tool changer’s mysterious little brother.

The Bambu Lab P3C combo is a tool changer with room for seven tools and a 256 x 256 x 260mm build volume, roughly the same as the P2S. It ships as either a five-tool unit, with two empty slots for later customization, or as a seven-tool “multi-material combo” with six 1.75mm tools and one 2.85mm tool. Bambu is bringing back old school 2.85mm filament in the form of super squishy TPU 75A.

The five-tool unit is priced at $1,149, while the seven-tool is launching at $1,299.

It offers the same excellent TPU printing process for both standard and phat TPU and has rapidly joined the select group of send it and forget it printers in my fleet. I’ve had very few failures, even when printing more technical filaments.

Industry observers note that the P3C is not quite as tall as the H3C, but it does require almost 4ft (1,212 mm) of vertical space for the AMS lid to fully open. So initiative accordingly and have a good space picked out in advance.

According to recent reports, bambu’s most annoying cost-saving measure took the A right out of AMS. There’s no motor of any sort in the AMS 3P, leaving you to manually load and unload the filament all the way to the nozzle. The process takes a long time if you are loading all of the filament slots. The upside of not having powered rollers is that the AMS 3P will run almost any 1kg or smaller spool without issue.

In a recent development, the printer can run different-sized nozzles from .2 mm to .8 mm, and has an optional 2.85 mm TPU filament tool. The FlexFeed extruder with Active Grip Control just pushes whatever filament it’s asked to while changing on the fly. It may be the best extruder I’ve reviewed, however, the printer as a whole is not quite what we need for the best 3D printers of 2026.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that the Bambu Lab P3C comes with five .4mm tools preinstalled in the bottom of the AMS 3P. Also included are a toolkit and cables needed to assemble the printer, along with quick start guides for both the printer and AMS 3P, and a few spare parts. It does not come with a USB memory stick, which is needed for recording time lapses.

We received the multi-material combo for review, which came with five tools installed, plus two additional tools I had to set up myself (one 1.75mm and one 2.85mm), along with several spools of PLA Palette and 2.85mm TPU 75A.

The P3C is missing several perks of the bigger H3C in order to save costs and keep the price reasonable. The most disappointing is the lack of a motor to drive the filament spools. This makes the “A” in the AMS 3P questionable, as you are forced to manually feed the filament all the way to the nozzle, as well as handle retraction when unloading.

The AMS 3P also does not come with a filament drier, although an optional 75C dryer will be available for $159.90.

According to recent reports, the basic Bambu Lab P3C comes standard with only five tools and is expandable to seven. The Swaptek system keeps the cooling fans and extruder on the toolhead, with each tool having its own filament path, heater, and a hardened steel nozzle. When printing, the idle tools are preheated, allowing for extremely fast tool swaps.

The nozzles on each tool can be swapped out with different sizes, and multiple sizes can be used in the same print.

Bambu Lab will also release tools for cutting, drawing, debossing, and foil transfer in the future.

The Bambu Lab P3C supports printing TPU with a bypass port on all filament slots except 2 and 6, which allows TPU to skip the tube, reducing friction. If you have the optional 2.85mm tool, you can mount it to any slot with a bypass.

Please note that the 2.85mm tool has a wider filament path – it's not just the nozzle tip that changes dimensions.

The tools dock on a rack in front of the printer which retracts after each tool change, allowing for a clear view of the build plate.

Industry observers note that the Flexfeed extruder is impressive. It switches from 1.75mm to 2.85mm filament on the fly and uses what Bambu Lab calls Active Grip Control with feedback from the extruder motor.

Like the H3C, there are magnetic covers on the left and right sides of the AMS and a front cover that attaches in slots to allow easy access to the chamber for maintenance. The front cover is a bit tricky, and you need to lift the AMS up to get it free. For this reason, I didn’t bother to secure the AMS to the base of the printer. You really need to remove that front panel to change out the tools.

Changing tools is one of the few frustrating things about the Bambu Lab P3C (or the H3C, as it’s the same process). There is very little room to work, and there are sharp plastic edges that left me bloodied on one occasion. I would suggest picking your favorite configuration and leaving it there if you can.

The AMS is massive and requires a lot of additional vertical space to fully open the lid to get at the spools. Bambu Lab recommends a clearance of 1,212 mm or almost four feet from the base in order to open the lid. Surprisingly, this smaller P3C is only 3.58 inches shorter than the major H3C. With the printer sitting on a standard countertop, a step-stool will be mandatory equipment for most people. Bambu offers a rolling cart for the H3C that puts the printer at a more manageable height, and I would highly recommend getting it for the P3C.

Industry observers note that the base unit of the Bambu Lab P3C looks similar to the P and X series printers, with a plastic outer frame and a steel chassis. The build plate is a standard 256 x 256 mm, with 260 mm available on the Z-axis. The P3C does not have active chamber heating, but being enclosed with a max of 300C on the nozzle and 110C on the bed, it has the ability to print many of the more common technical filaments. The chamber is ventilated with HEPA and active carbon filtration.

Industry observers note that the 3D printer has a great camera, which is used for AI detection and monitoring using the Bambu Handy app and the device page of Bambu Slicer. The camera can produce time-lapses of your prints but does require a USB memory stick to store them.

Recent findings suggest that the Bambu Lab P3C and AMS 3P ship in separate boxes but are almost fully assembled. After removing the packaging, there are two screws holding the dock retainers that need to be removed and 6 screws securing the bed in place.

There is a helpful reminder to do this when the printer is first turned on. AMS 3P is mounted on top of the printer and requires a good deal of vertical space. There are four screws to attach the AMS 3P to the printer, but I left these off since the front panel of the AMS is easier to remove when you can tip the AMS back a little.

The individual tools attach to the dock magnetically and must be placed manually, which can take a little fiddling to get used to.

The touch screen attaches to the front of the printer without tools, and the ribbon cable to connect it is just long enough to work.

It has been revealed that the Bambu Lab P3C levels its bed as part of its initial calibration and again at the start of every print. The system works perfectly.

The Bambu Lab P3C does not have auto-loading, as there is no motor.

When loading multiple upcoming filaments for a print, the process can take a while and is very hands-on. When using normal 1.75 mm filament, the material is pushed into the orange tube in the AMS when called for by the printer.

When using TPU, either 1.75mm or 2.85 filament, drop the filament into a slot with a bypass port in the bottom and drag it by hand to the tool. The normal Bowden tube must be removed from the tool and clipped to the side. When running 1.75mm TPU a short piece of bowden tube must be inserted into the tool to help feed the filament correctly. The 2.85mm TPU doesn’t need the short tube and can feed directly.

The printer has a helpful filament guide to walk you through the loading operation.

Bambu Lab-branded filament with RFID tags will automatically enter the filament type and color. Other brands must be entered manually via the printer’s touchscreen.

Unloading filament is the reverse of loading. You’ll need to manually retract material once it is cut by the printer. There is a batch unloading command that will allow you to wait until all of the selected filaments have been cut.

In a recent development, bambu Studio is based on PrusaSlicer and its predecessors. New for the P3C and the H3C is the ability to mix different tool sizes. It is one of the best slicers available with good filament mapping, control and print monitoring, with access to Makerworld, Bambu Lab’s file sharing service.

It has been revealed that the P3C does not come with filament samples. Bambu Lab sent a few spools of their latest PLA Palette and 2.85mm 75A TPU to try. Be sure to check out our best filaments for 3D printing to fill up your AMS 3P.

It has been revealed that this print of Carl and Donut from the Dungeon Crawler Carl book series took 15 hours and 35 minutes to print using a .16mm layer height for smooth detail. I used the default settings, but slowed the outer walls to 65mm/s. The print is exceptionally good, though the supports left a few marks under horizontal areas like the arms and shin. Normally I’d tilt a model this back 45 degrees to save time and support, but the fin on this particular model is vexing and would have added an hour to the print time and another 10g of support.

This is printed in seven colors of PLA, maxing out the P3C slots. Polymaker HT-PLA Pro White, Prusament Galaxy Black and Galaxy Silver PLA, Elegoo PLA Brown and Silk Red, Inland Bone White, and Matterhacker’s Purple MH Build Series PLA.

It has been revealed that printing with seven colors allows you more creative freedom when printing complex models. Though the brown did a lot of heavy lifting on this print, I think the P3C really captured Carl nicely.

I tried some of Bambu Lab’s matte PETG on a Cute Blue Jay from Makerworld. Since the model prints best straight up and down, and requires pretty extensive supports, I used a scrap of Prusa Lipstick Red PLA as an interface layer.

Industry observers note that using a .16mm layer height, the print took 8 hours and 55 minutes running at a little under 100mm/s on average. The matte PETG makes the model look like it was painted. This is printed in black, white and baby blue matte PETG and the supports came off with no residue what so ever.

Sources indicate that though the P3C doesn’t get hot enough to print PPS, it does print most PA, PC, and PET filaments very well. I printed a spool and a half of Sunlu Easy PA, making all of the mechanical parts for two radio-controlled Death Racers. Initially, I made just a few items per plate, but with just a little glue stick, the bed adhesion was so good that I felt comfortable loading up the plates as full as possible and had zero failures. All were printed with a .2mm layer height and slowed to 100mm/s by me in the slicer. Other than a tiny bit of stringing, the parts are perfect mechanically.

The Bambu Lab P3C’s HEPA filter does a good job filtering the stinkier filaments like ABS and ASA. I printed this wire holding vice using Fusion ABS matte ionized cobalt black and Prusa lipstick red ASA.

This is printed with a .2 mm layer height and an average print speed of 120mm/s. The entire print took a little less than 2 hours and 3 minutes, and the parts fit together perfectly.

With the H3C and now the P3C, I have seen the future of printing with TPU. The AMS 3P bypass ports are just the ticket for printing soft materials.

Sources indicate that I printed several plates of treads for my RC Death Racer project. Normally, I print these a few at a time to limit the fallout from print failures, but this proved unnecessary. I ran 48 treads in Bambu Lab Cyan 2.85mm TPU 75A and another 48 using Bambu Lab 90A TPU. Both prints used a .2mm layer height and were limited to 100 mm/s in the slicer. The 75A print finished a little quicker at 19 hours 10 minutes, with the 90A filament taking 19 hours and 40 minutes.

Both are terrific prints with no stringing at all and zero failures.

The P3C can print almost any filament I own beautifully. It lacks a few creature comforts like auto-loading, filament drying (which can be upgraded), and a heated chamber. It’s also tall enough to require a step stool to load those back filament slots.

The Bambu Lab P3C is best for anyone who wants poop-free multicolor, multi-material printing without paying H3C money. I highly recommend it for anyone who looks to print a lot of TPU and doesn’t need that larger build plate. If you can live without the automatic feeding you normally get from a Bambu printer, then the money you’ll save in filament is worth the hassle.

Industry observers note that this machine gives you most of the advantages of the Bambu Lab H3C at roughly half the $2,499 price tag. The open-source four-color Snapmaker U1 is still worth it right now while it’s on sale for $699. Another option is the Creality K3, which is another four-color tool changer with a similar build size for $849.

Industry observers note that denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for Democrats eyeing the White House, President Donald Trump’s coziness with tech executives was already a potent target even before he successfully pressured Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive.Now his extraordinary intervention has crystallized their concerns about the growing power of artificial intelligence companies and his blending of government and business interests.Huang had lost his job because of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing. Eleven days later, Nvidia’s board put him back in charge.Although Democrats lack a unified vision for how to handle the proliferation of artificial intelligence, the episode was an opportunity for them to speak largely in unison as they called Huang’s return a threat to national security and described Trump’s role as corrupt.Nvidia’s decision sends a message “that the national security of this country is not as crucial as your relationship with President Trump,” said Sen. Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat considering a White House campaign, in an interview with The Associated Press.“We also have to figure out how corporate America doesn’t take a bad lesson from this, and thinks that somehow it’s OK for them to evade national security for the purposes of just selling more,” Gallego said.Nvidia is under scrutiny over whether it’s complying with U.S. restrictions on the export of its most advanced semiconductors to China and their use by Chinese tech firms.The manufacturer’s share price dropped sharply during Huang’s brief absence, dragging down the broader stock market to one of its worst weeks since the 2008 financial crisis, before recovering with Monday’s announcement of his reinstatement. Trump argues that Huang’s leadership at Nvidia is necessary Still euphoric over their sweeping midterm victories, many ambitious Democrats are still feeling around for the right message on artificial intelligence, which carries both promise and peril as it becomes increasingly intertwined with the economy, infrastructure and daily life.Trump’s intervention put a spotlight on his own financial stake in the company, which his latest financial disclosure report indicates was worth at least $12.5 million at the end of 2025, and on the millions of dollars Huang contributed to Trump’s ballroom project.Writing on social media that “rules should apply to everyone,” California Rep. Ro Khanna noted that “the rich & powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price.”Trump worried that Huang’s ouster was not only tanking the stock market but also risked putting the U.S. behind Beijing in the race for tech dominance.“I’m doing it for the country,” Trump said on CNBC.Huang’s reinstatement reinforced the message, which many Democrats delivered in the midterms, that the system is rigged against average Americans, said Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project and a former aide to Democrats. Substantial tech leaders can be a powerful foil.“They are the most unlikeable men in America, and yet it seems like the system is working very well for them,” Haworth said. “The news this week just reinforced that idea. So the mission that Democrats have now is to continue to prove to voters that they are fighting against this corrupt system, against the influence of tech CEOs and on behalf of Americans.”Nvidia’s board and Trump himself left no ambiguity over who drove the decision.It was based on input from “senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia said in a press release announcing Huang’s return.Trump said in an interview with CNBC that “I spoke to them, let me just put it that way. And I convinced them.” Democratic candidates see corruption, security risks Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro tied Huang’s reinstatement to “the sheer corruption and weakness” of the president, calling it “another example of the dangerous combination governing this country: a rigged system that protects those at the very top no matter what, and a corrupt White House that cannot be trusted to put the economic well-being and safety of American families first.”Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan said that Trump’s pressure campaign made clear that, to the president, “making money is more important than America’s national security or the rule of law.”Slotkin, a former CIA analyst, added, “If ever there was an glitch that deserved national security oversight, it’s this one.”And Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker drew a comparison between Huang’s reinstatement and Democrats’ broad wins in this month’s midterm elections, calling the CEO’s return an example of “the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected.”Pritzker urged Democrats “to speak with one voice and not be afraid to fight the Trump administration,” saying Trump and Vice President JD Vance “will move mountains for tech billionaires.” —Jonathan J. Cooper and Meg Kinnard, Associated Press.

For Democrats eyeing the White House, President Donald Trump’s coziness with tech executives was already a potent target even before he successfully pressured Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive.Now his extraordinary intervention has crystallized their concerns about the growing power of artificial intelligence companies and his blending of government and business interests.Huang had lost his job because of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing. Eleven days later, Nvidia’s board put him back in charge.Although Democrats lack a unified vision for how to handle the proliferation of artificial intelligence, the episode was an opportunity for them to speak largely in unison as they called Huang’s return a threat to national security and described Trump’s role as corrupt.Nvidia’s decision sends a message “that the national security of this country is not as vital as your relationship with President Trump,” mentioned Sen. Ruben Gallego, an Arizona Democrat considering a White House campaign, in an interview with The Associated Press.“We also have to figure out how corporate America doesn’t take a bad lesson from this, and thinks that somehow it’s OK for them to evade national security for the purposes of just selling more,” Gallego said.Nvidia is under scrutiny over whether it’s complying with U.S. restrictions on the export of its most advanced semiconductors to China and their use by Chinese tech firms.The organization’s share price dropped sharply during Huang’s brief absence, dragging down the broader stock market to one of its worst weeks since the 2008 financial crisis, before recovering with Monday’s announcement of his reinstatement.

Still euphoric over their sweeping midterm victories, many ambitious Democrats are still feeling around for the right message on artificial intelligence, which carries both promise and peril as it becomes increasingly intertwined with the economy, infrastructure and daily life.Trump’s intervention put a spotlight on his own financial stake in the tech giant, which his latest financial disclosure report notes was worth at least $12.5 million at the end of 2025, and on the millions of dollars Huang contributed to Trump’s ballroom project.Writing on social media that “rules should apply to everyone,” California Rep. Ro Khanna noted that “the rich & powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price.”Trump worried that Huang’s ouster was not only tanking the stock market but also risked putting the U.S. behind Beijing in the race for tech dominance.“I’m doing it for the country,” Trump noted on CNBC.Huang’s reinstatement reinforced the message, which many Democrats delivered in the midterms, that the system is rigged against average Americans, said Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project and a former aide to Democrats. Major tech leaders can be a powerful foil.“They are the most unlikeable men in America, and yet it seems like the system is working very well for them,” Haworth said. “The news this week just reinforced that idea. So the mission that Democrats have now is to continue to prove to voters that they are fighting against this corrupt system, against the influence of tech CEOs and on behalf of Americans.”Nvidia’s board and Trump himself left no ambiguity over who drove the decision.It was based on input from “senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia said in a press release announcing Huang’s return.Trump said in an interview with CNBC that “I spoke to them, let me just put it that way. And I convinced them.”.

Recent findings suggest that pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro tied Huang’s reinstatement to “the sheer corruption and weakness” of the president, calling it “another example of the dangerous combination governing this country: a rigged system that protects those at the very top no matter what, and a corrupt White House that cannot be trusted to put the economic well-being and safety of American families first.”Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan said that Trump’s pressure campaign made clear that, to the president, “making money is more important than America’s national security or the rule of law.”Slotkin, a former CIA analyst, added, “If ever there was an issue that deserved national security oversight, it’s this one.”And Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker drew a comparison between Huang’s reinstatement and Democrats’ broad wins in this month’s midterm elections, calling the CEO’s return an example of “the greed and lack of accountability that the country just rejected.”Pritzker urged Democrats “to speak with one voice and not be afraid to fight the Trump administration,” saying Trump and Vice President JD Vance “will move mountains for tech billionaires.”.

—Jonathan J. Cooper and Meg Kinnard, Associated Press.

In a recent development, the announcement immediately drew attention because of how far apart the two product categories are. #116527. What is Model Routing in AI?
