Breaking: AI upended entry-level jobs. Here’s what employers are actually looking for

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room.
  • AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room.
  • A recent survey of nearly 7,000 workers, managers, and executives found that 51% believe AI is reducing early-career opportunities, while 49% say tasks that traditionally helped employees build work experience are increasingly being handled by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room. Many are placing the blame on AI for making tasks in many entry-level jobs outdated; data seems to back that up. A recent survey of nearly 7,000 workers, managers, and executives found that 51% believe AI is reducing early-career opportunities, while 49% say tasks that traditionally helped employees build work experience are increasingly being handled by AI. Another shows that entry-level listings have plummeted 35% since 2023; another suggests entry-level jobs in Newly introduced York City have been cut in half. That means the pressure is on for early-career candidates to show employers what they can bring to a role beyond their ability to use AI tools. A catch-22 emerges: many employers increasingly turn to AI, yet many also want candidates who can think independently, come up with original ideas, recognize when to put the technology aside and trust their own judgment. Indeed, many young workers find themselves in a tricky-to-navigate, even unfair entry-level job market. Luckily, there are tips that can make you stand out in a labor market that both increasingly relies on AI, and that also demands workers show employers the human skills they’re looking for. Don’t let AI write your resume for you Sure, AI can be a helpful writing tool: it can help you brainstorm, organize your experience, even give you a first draft. But if every candidate is using AI to write their application, it can become harder to show what makes you different. According to Amitoj Sandhu, Manager of Global Early Talent at HR platform Dayforce, employers are starting to see more applications that all sound alike. “Every single profile looks the same. They all are the same on the paper, so it becomes really hard for us to shortlist them and present in front of leaders,” he claims. Sandhu says AI is a useful starting point, but candidates need to be able to use their own voice, and  stand behind what they submit. After all, if AI is writing your resume for you, when it comes time for the interview, “will you be able to validate the results?” he says. Sandhu recommends preparing two or three strong examples from internships, school projects, or extracurricular activities that you can actually speak to authentically without farming everything out to ChatGPT. Then, be ready to walk an interviewer through those experiences and what you learned from them. With fewer entry-level roles apparently available, layering this in can make your application pop. Do use AI in your cover letter, but with caution “AI can be a great tool for writing a better cover letter. It can help candidates organize their ideas, communicate more clearly and make meaningful connections between their own interests and the company they’re applying to,” says Dan Kejsefman, Talent Director at Avature, a software development company. He says AI can raise the bar in terms of an application’s quality—but at the same time, “the motivation behind it still needs to be genuine.”  “I’d encourage candidates to start with their own reasons for wanting the job: What interests them about the company? What would they like to learn? What experiences or interests connect them to the opportunity? Then use AI to help communicate those ideas more effectively,” he says. The crucial thing is being able to explain and stand behind what’s in your cover letter. “AI can help you tell your story better,” he says, “but the story still has to be yours.” Use AI tools where you can—many jobs will expect you to use them to some extent, anyway—but standing out in an increasingly crowded entry-level field means tapping into what makes you, you. Don’t leave your curiosity at home According to Sandhu, when it comes time for the interview, curiosity is one of the biggest qualities employers look for. Missing that in an interview is “kind of a red flag for us,” Sandhu says. Sure, one way to demonstrate this is by researching the employer before the interview, and developing a genuine understanding of what the company does and the industry it operates in. But preparation is only part of it. Kejsefman says candidates also need to show genuine interest in the conversation, rather than simply relying on a list of questions prepared with AI during your interview practice. “AI can help candidates research a company, understand a role, and prepare thoughtful questions. That’s useful, and I wouldn’t discourage it,” Kejsefman explains. “But there’s a difference between asking an impressive question, and actually being interested in understanding the answer.” For example, curious candidates listen carefully, ask follow-up questions and try to understand why things work the way they do. That’s a timeless strategy, regardless of AI or not. Young workers “don’t necessarily have all the answers, and that’s perfectly fine, especially early in their careers. What matters is whether they show a real desire to learn and understand,” Kejsefman says. Do bring your own judgment to the work Sandhu says employers want candidates who can question the information AI provides, apply their own judgment and build on what the technology produces. Think of a software developer who might use ChatGPT to generate code, but still needs to determine whether it makes sense or meets the requirements or passes the right tests. Human judgment, after all, has long been touted as something that will still prove crucial in the AI era—in fact, as more decisions get outsourced to robots, it becomes even more valuable. “Can you use your own judgment to evaluate a response you get from AI? Can you build on that context? That’s what we’re looking for,” Sandhu says. In fields such as communications and journalism, employers still want to see creativity and original ideas rather than generic content generated by AI. “They want to look at how you think and what kind of ideas you can spark, not just all the generic ideas AI is producing,” Sandhu says. Kejsefman says AI adoption is still uneven across organizations, creating an opportunity for early-career professionals. A recent graduate who develops strong AI skills can bring something valuable to a team, even when working alongside people with much more professional experience. But they also bring enthusiasm and perspective older workers don’t have, and that robots definitely don’t have. Kejsefman also cautions against focusing exclusively on learning individual AI tools. As those tools continue to change, the ability to think critically, understand problems and evaluate results will become increasingly important. As AI takes on more workplace tasks, your ability to bring your own ideas, judgment and perspective to the work can help you stand out—especially when looking to break into a field or organization. Do prioritize experience over job titles Regardless of best practices, as AI continues to change the skills employers need, recent graduates may need to be more flexible about where they start their careers. For starters, Sandhu cautions against focusing too heavily on a particular job title or starting salary. “The significant mistake which they’re making is they’re running after titles and what the compensation is going to look like,” Sandhu says. Instead, he encouraged candidates to prioritize gaining experience and finding opportunities to get started, even if the position isn’t exactly what they initially envisioned or in their precisely preferred field. “Don’t run after a specific job title in the world which is changing every day,” he says. And that experience doesn’t have to come from a traditional job. Kejsefman encourages recent graduates to draw on those other past experiences, like university projects or volunteering—even personal projects or side gigs, which a lot of Gen Z already has anyway. “They need examples of situations where they’ve taken initiative, faced a problem, learned something new, or adapted when things didn’t go as expected,” Kejsefman says. “For someone starting their career, demonstrating that mindset can be much more valuable than presenting a perfectly polished result.” Make no mistake—for new workers in the workplace, it’s rough out there. But keeping these strategies, which mix time-tested tactics with AI adoption and adaptation, could open the right door at the right time.

AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room. Many are placing the blame on AI for making tasks in many entry-level jobs outdated; data seems to back that up.

A recent survey of nearly 7,000 workers, managers, and executives found that 51% believe AI is reducing early-career opportunities, while 49% say tasks that traditionally helped employees build work experience are increasingly being handled by AI. Another shows that entry-level listings have plummeted 35% since 2023; another suggests entry-level jobs in New York City have been cut in half.

Recent findings suggest that that means the pressure is on for early-career candidates to show employers what they can bring to a role beyond their ability to use AI tools. A catch-22 emerges: many employers increasingly turn to AI, yet many also want candidates who can think independently, come up with original ideas, recognize when to put the technology aside and trust their own judgment.

In a recent development, indeed, many young workers find themselves in a tricky-to-navigate, even unfair entry-level job market. Luckily, there are tips that can make you stand out in a labor market that both increasingly relies on AI, and that also demands workers show employers the human skills they’re looking for.

Sure, AI can be a helpful writing tool: it can help you brainstorm, organize your experience, even give you a first draft. But if every candidate is using AI to write their application, it can become harder to show what makes you different. According to Amitoj Sandhu, Manager of Global Early Talent at HR platform Dayforce, employers are starting to see more applications that all sound alike.

“Every single profile looks the same. They all are the same on the paper, so it becomes really hard for us to shortlist them and present in front of leaders,” he says.

It has been revealed that sandhu claims AI is a useful starting point, but candidates need to be able to use their own voice, and  stand behind what they submit. After all, if AI is writing your resume for you, when it comes time for the interview, “will you be able to validate the results?” he says.

Sandhu recommends preparing two or three strong examples from internships, school projects, or extracurricular activities that you can actually speak to authentically without farming everything out to ChatGPT. Then, be ready to walk an interviewer through those experiences and what you learned from them.

With fewer entry-level roles apparently available, layering this in can make your application pop.

Industry observers note that “AI can be a great tool for writing a better cover letter. It can help candidates organize their ideas, communicate more clearly and make meaningful connections between their own interests and the organization they’re applying to,” says Dan Kejsefman, Talent Director at Avature, a software development company.

He claims AI can raise the bar in terms of an application’s quality—but at the same time, “the motivation behind it still needs to be genuine.”.

“I’d encourage candidates to start with their own reasons for wanting the job: What interests them about the company? What would they like to learn? What experiences or interests connect them to the opportunity? Then use AI to help communicate those ideas more effectively,” he notes.

The notable thing is being able to explain and stand behind what’s in your cover letter.

“AI can help you tell your story better,” he indicates, “but the story still has to be yours.” Use AI tools where you can—many jobs will expect you to use them to some extent, anyway—but standing out in an increasingly crowded entry-level field means tapping into what makes you, you.

According to Sandhu, when it comes time for the interview, curiosity is one of the biggest qualities employers look for. Missing that in an interview is “kind of a red flag for us,” Sandhu claims.

Sure, one way to demonstrate this is by researching the employer before the interview, and developing a genuine understanding of what the organization does and the industry it operates in. But preparation is only part of it.

Kejsefman claims candidates also need to show genuine interest in the conversation, rather than simply relying on a list of questions prepared with AI during your interview practice.

“AI can help candidates research a manufacturer, understand a role, and prepare thoughtful questions. That’s useful, and I wouldn’t discourage it,” Kejsefman explains. “But there’s a difference between asking an impressive question, and actually being interested in understanding the answer.”.

For example, curious candidates listen carefully, ask follow-up questions and try to understand why things work the way they do. That’s a timeless strategy, regardless of AI or not.

Recent findings suggest that young workers “don’t necessarily have all the answers, and that’s perfectly fine, especially early in their careers. What matters is whether they show a real desire to learn and understand,” Kejsefman says.

Sandhu indicates employers want candidates who can question the information AI provides, apply their own judgment and build on what the technology produces.

Recent findings suggest that think of a software developer who might use ChatGPT to generate code, but still needs to determine whether it makes sense or meets the requirements or passes the right tests. Human judgment, after all, has long been touted as something that will still prove crucial in the AI era—in fact, as more decisions get outsourced to robots, it becomes even more valuable.

“Can you use your own judgment to evaluate a response you get from AI? Can you build on that context? That’s what we’re looking for,” Sandhu notes.

In fields such as communications and journalism, employers still want to see creativity and original ideas rather than generic content generated by AI. “They want to look at how you think and what kind of ideas you can spark, not just all the generic ideas AI is producing,” Sandhu indicates.

Sources indicate that kejsefman says AI adoption is still uneven across organizations, creating an opportunity for early-career professionals. A recent graduate who develops strong AI skills can bring something valuable to a team, even when working alongside people with much more professional experience. But they also bring enthusiasm and perspective older workers don’t have, and that robots definitely don’t have.

Kejsefman also cautions against focusing exclusively on learning individual AI tools. As those tools continue to change, the ability to think critically, understand problems and evaluate results will become increasingly crucial.

As AI takes on more workplace tasks, your ability to bring your own ideas, judgment and perspective to the work can help you stand out—especially when looking to break into a field or organization.

“The big mistake which they’re making is they’re running after titles and what the compensation is going to look like,” Sandhu notes.

Instead, he encouraged candidates to prioritize gaining experience and finding opportunities to get started, even if the position isn’t exactly what they initially envisioned or in their precisely preferred field.

“Don’t run after a specific job title in the world which is changing every day,” he notes.

It has been revealed that and that experience doesn’t have to come from a traditional job. Kejsefman encourages recent graduates to draw on those other past experiences, like university projects or volunteering—even personal projects or side gigs, which a lot of Gen Z already has anyway.

“They need examples of situations where they’ve taken initiative, faced a problem, learned something latest, or adapted when things didn’t go as expected,” Kejsefman claims.

“For someone starting their career, demonstrating that mindset can be much more valuable than presenting a perfectly polished result.”.

#116508. Latest Update: Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1795 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.
  • Many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout.
  • The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.

Many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout. After last night's driving around I would also maybe add in a quick bonus one, come to think of it: watch out for cyclists making last-minute left turns. Or don't, actually. Half of this lot deserve it….

The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh. Though naturally I do explain the way some parts of this game work, taking away some of the sense of discovery. You can take my word for it that there's plenty more to discover beyond this though, so worry not.

If you'd like even more help navigating Leonida, then check out our wonderful guide team's GTA 6 walkthrough.

The number one thing I'd tell people to do in GTA 6 is to create lots of save files and, as you progress and start needing to overwrite them, to try to keep a roughly even spread of files through each chapter. There are various reasons for this - for one, while the game autosaves, it doesn't seem to do that successfully if you suddenly lose power to the console or witness a rare game crash, so it'll preserve your progress. More than that: GTA's story and missions are surprisingly, perhaps mysteriously reactive. Quite a lot can differ, and so being able to go back and make different choices, or play the game differently, will be something 'future you' likely appreciates.

In a recent development, in the very early game you won't have access to a bank account, but once you do: you should put every bit of cash you have in there as soon as you can. Cash is lost on death or arrest - which can happen quite often in GTA 6, funnily enough - and there's no real benefit to carrying it around. Just about everything, besides in-game strippers, can be paid for via your BuckMe account directly. And there's a relatively low $20,000 limit you really don't want to hit in the middle of raiding a gang hideout, either.

GTA 6 has a luxurious range of customisation settings, from hiding notifications about your relationship to reinstating the old 'tap to sprint' control scheme. The accessibility settings - while crucially I'm not an expert - seem considerable. And there are somewhat disguised difficult settings here around enemy damage taken and encounters with the police.

Fairly early in the game you'll gain access to the Scooter Bros. App, which lets you repair or summon your owned vehicles at will. Crucially, there's also an option to pay a one-off fee to unlock three free uses of the app per day. At $12,000, in the early game this is a lot of dosh, but once you rack up that kind of money after advancing through the game a little, it's well worth the initial cost. The sooner you unlock it, the more value it provides over time on a cost-per-use basis. And trust me when I say: as the game's intensity ramps up, you will probably find yourself needing to repair and recover your vehicles quite often. (Also, in Chapter 1, before you get access to the app, you can access the same service by going to your phone's contacts and calling Joey - handy!).

Rockstar has somewhat disincentivised it by adding a cost and putting it in your phone's apps rather than the main map screen, but you can fast travel around Leonida if you ever want or need to. This is done via the RideMe Uber-like app. It's not cheap - you'll need to pay both the fee for the journey and an additional $100 to skip that journey and instantly arrive at your destination, but in certain scenarios it might prove useful. To skip the journey, hold L2/LT once in the cab, and then hold down Triangle/Y when the option is shown. However….

While it's possible to journey-skip your way around this world, having tested that first hand I'd advise against it. It might be obvious, but GTA 6 is genuinely designed around you manually travelling around, typically in the car. If you skip all your commutes between missions or locations, you'll miss out on the game's dozens and dozens of emergent events, which lead to anything from one-off jokes to entire mission chains. The car is also, in a way, kind of the heart of the entire game. Relish the intentional slowness!

Industry observers note that again, avoiding spoilers here, but in the mid game the 'true' loop of GTA 6 gameplay will properly reveal itself, in all the many methods of earning money and the increased emphasis on doing so. You can of course play the game however you like, but having reached the end and looked back from that point, I found that if there was a particular moment to set aside as the time for aimlessly exploring the world, it was from around Chapter 3 onwards. You'll have enough tools to be able to see it at more or less its fullest then, but also won't have missed anything essential by waiting until that point to take your foot off the pedal either.

Industry observers note that A handy early-game tip here that even I missed when I was playing, but have since discovered: two islands in the small cluster of them to the south-west of Jason's early game home each house a really useful weapon, in a silenced pistol and a handy shotgun. You'll own these permanently once found, and so they can be incredibly helpful for navigating missions with maximum or minimal violence. Look for shipwrecks on those islands to find them. The pistol is hidden under a little hatch on the deck of a shipwreck on the southernmost point of the south-easternmost island. The shotgun is next to a small wooden wrecked boat around the middle of the northernmost island.

Recent findings suggest that A mechanic I slightly underused at first was the ability to 'save' a given outfit to your car. You can do this either from your car's trunk or from the wardrobe, and it's hugely useful as you start to get into more elaborate scrapes with the police (and also if you just like to role-play a bit and don the right outfit for the right occasion).

According to recent reports, there are lots of reasons for this, from the moments of intimacy it affords you with your partner, to the extra buffs you can get from resting. Sleep at home, for instance, and you can then immediately pet your snake (ahem), down a coffee or drink from the fridge, grab an apple and take a shower for a range of buffs across health, stamina, and focus. Each of these will last quite some time, so it's worth the few minutes of time to do them. Eating and drinking regularly also helps you maximise gains in the gym.

Rockstar seems to enjoy the concept of a game within a game, and that's exemplified well by the in-game phone. You can find missions via scrolling Snapmatic, it's in-game social media, or from texting various contacts you pick up as the game progresses. It's worth checking it every now and then just to see if anything interesting - or just funny or absurd - might pop up.

According to recent reports, car trunks, both those belonging to the public and the police, are often well worth a look. Even if you're quickly nabbing a car for a short-term dash, take a moment to check the boot for anything worthwhile. We've found everything from sellable narcotics to very useful weapons in there. In cop cars, that goes up several notches, too.

Industry observers note that A small thing, but in-mission checkpoints are relatively generous in GTA 6. If you really wanted to complete a mission a certain way - undetected or non-violent, say - then don't be afraid to quickly re-load rather than feeling you need to manually load up an earlier save, or give up on your goal entirely. It's also helped me out with a few minor progress-jamming bugs along the way too.

This might seem obvious, but it's worth emphasising for early-game players: it's very, very rare that you actually need to kill anybody in GTA 6. Enemies are fully incapacitated when you see a yellow hit marker over your crosshairs, even if that just comes from blasting away at their toes. If you make a habit of navigating combat this way then that also makes it much easier to recover your 'Professional' criminal status if you ever do decide to go full rampage. Though you can, of course, ultimately play this game however you like. Just be aware there may be consequences, known and unknown, as you go. Also: don't forget to click the right analog stick to aim down sights - it's an easy thing to forget when playing a third-person shooter like this, and not always the best way to operate, but incredibly helpful in select circumstances.

In a recent development, throughout the game you'll have a 'family savings' goal to hit. As you progress you'll find more ways to earn money much faster, and so it's easy to make up for lost time here if, later on, you decide that actually you do want to think about the future after all. But that grind will be a fair bit less painful if you chip away at the target as you go. As long as you save yourself some fun money - a few hundred in the early game, few thousand in the mid game, and a few tens of thousands late on - then you'll have enough to do key things like buying latest garages to register vehicles, or paying to register them themselves.

Sources indicate that throughout your time with GTA 6 you'll encounter moments when you need to make a choice. Interestingly, I noticed at least a few occasions where a scenario changed when I just waited, doing nothing at all. Sometimes that might mean a choice is made for you - so waiting is a risk - but on other occasions upcoming options become available. Sometimes they might mean a genuinely different consequence, others they might just lead to characters reacting in a certain kind of way. But it's worth experimenting - your first options aren't always your only ones.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Costco is coming to the rescue of anyone scrambling to put together a last-minute Thanksgiving dinner, bringing back its affordable meal kit with enough food to feed up to eight people.

Earlier in November, Costco made headlines for selling a massive 30-pound Thanksgiving dinner for $200, complete with a turkey, numerous sides, and desserts.

However, that extravagant feast required customers to place their orders by November 13, leaving anyone who missed the deadline out of luck.

Thankfully, with just days to go until Thanksgiving, Costco has brought back a considerably cheaper alternative that doesn’t require a pre-order.

A post shared by Laura Jayne Lamb (@costcohotfinds).

As reported by Delish, Costco’s Kirkland Signature Turkey Dinner Kit has returned to the retailer’s deli department for 2026.

Each kit comes with a seasoned, boneless half turkey breast, herbed stuffing, Yukon Gold mashed potatoes, green beans, cranberry sauce, and gravy.

The kits are priced at $3.99 per pound and weigh around 10 pounds, meaning shoppers can expect to pay roughly $40 for the entire meal.

According to Costco’s official product listing, each kit serves seven to eight people, bringing the cost down to around $5 per person.

Recent findings suggest that while the turkey still needs to be cooked, much of the preparation has already been taken care of. The meat even comes sitting on top of the stuffing, allowing the juices to soak into it while roasting.

Unlike Costco’s more expensive Thanksgiving feast, however, the kit doesn’t include dinner rolls or dessert, so you might want to grab one of the retailer’s famous pumpkin pies while you’re there.

Costco isn’t the only retailer trying to make Thanksgiving more affordable. Walmart is offering a $35 feast that feeds 10 people, while Amazon has a $25 Thanksgiving meal with same-day delivery on qualifying orders.

Costco is selling a massive 30-pound Thanksgiving dinner for $200, but you have to pre-order it.

Walmart takes on Costco and Amazon with $35 Thanksgiving feast that feeds 10 people.

Amazon announces $25 “complete” Thanksgiving meal with same-day delivery.

Both of those bundles primarily consist of groceries that customers will need to prepare themselves, giving Costco an advantage for anyone looking to spend less time in the kitchen.

Just don’t leave your shopping until Thanksgiving morning, as Costco’s warehouses will be closed on November 26.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It’s bad enough you have to sleep on the pull-out couch for a few days, but then come the questions.
  • If the topic of homeownership—and, more pointedly, why you don’t yet own a home—comes up at Thanksgiving, here’s a stat to keep your pestering relatives at bay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s bad enough you have to sleep on the pull-out couch for a few days, but then come the questions. If the topic of homeownership—and, more pointedly, why you don’t yet own a home—comes up at Thanksgiving, here’s a stat to keep your pestering relatives at bay. A household today earning a median income would need to save for 10.5 years to have enough for a 10% down payment on a median-priced home—that’s more than three times longer than in the 1980s, according to a new report from Realtor.com. While your relatives may bemoan the double-digit mortgage rates of the 1980s, homes on the market were relatively more affordable. That’s because the surge in home prices, and especially in recent years, has far outpaced the rise in wages, which is keeping many prospective homebuyers on the sidelines, according to the Austin-based real estate site. “The reality is that today’s aspiring buyers face a different housing market than generations before,” Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com, noted in a statement. And it’s not just that home prices have outpaced wage growth, homebuyers are also facing rising costs for insurance and homeowners association (HOA) fees that are stretching their budgets, she added. “The path to homeownership has become increasingly difficult.” In the 1980s, the median-priced home was selling for roughly 3.2 times the typical annual household income at the time, according to Realtor.com. Today, shoppers are trying to squeeze into a market where homes are selling for 4.8 times the typical household income. It’s no wonder, then, that so many younger people are living at home for longer to save up for a down payment when a first-time homebuyer is now 40 years old. WHERE HOUSING IS MORE, LESS AFFORDABLE Depending on where you live, you might already have an arsenal of mind-blowing stats about your local housing market. In some major metro areas, saving enough money for a down payment for a median-priced home has become a herculean task unto itself. People earning the median income could understandably feel locked out of the housing market in many areas. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the five where workers must save the longest for a 10% down payment on a median-priced home are:  Los Angeles, California: 24.8 years San Diego, California: 18.8 years San Jose, California: 18.4 years New York, New York: 17.0 years Boston, Massachusetts: 15.7 years On the flip side, saving up for a down payment in the following five metro areas could happen in the span of less than a decade for some households: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania: 7.2 years Detroit, Michigan: 7.6 years St. Louis, Missouri: 7.6 years Buffalo, New York: 7.9 years Cleveland, Ohio: 8.1 years Of course, housing-related costs aren’t limited to saving up for the down payment and then budgeting for monthly mortgage payments. Homeowners today must also factor in the rising costs of things like insurance or HOA fees at a time when the price of, well, everything seems to be going up. “For many younger Americans, the challenge isn’t a lack of willingness to save,” Jones said. “It’s that the financial goalposts have moved.”.

Tech Report: I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance.
  • Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal.
  • The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance. Voyaging uncharted waters may appear foolish to some, yet folly and heroism can often appear the same to the undiscerning eye," so states the voice of Johannes Zuch - creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' behind Leonida's latest favourite indie darling art game, Tenebrae Lux. It's pretentious, it's deeply up its own arse, and it's awkward and off-putting to play. A must-review for Eurogamer.

Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal. Jason is quick to dismiss Tenebrae Lux in manufacturer, but once Cal slinks off home - hungover and dreary - I slide the disc back into my JoyStation console and sink my teeth back into it. Jason loves this stuff, really. He only keeps Time Jackers: Rewind installed so his mates don't judge him.

The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name. It's Latin for 'darkness and light', or something similar. Is this riffing on Clair Obscur, which is French for 'light dark'? No, it's too cerebral for that - too plodding and navel-gazey. Sandfall Interactive wouldn't be this pretentious. Maybe it's a pastiche of Dear Esther, then, drawing on the tenets and schema of the 'walking simulator' genre and using that washed-out film noir aesthetic. But then, it's too wordy for that, with too many interactive and puzzle-adjacent elements. Ah, it must be mocking The Witness, instead - there's the telltale lighthouse, the 'I'm definitely not telling you where to go and what to do' internal narration, and of course the fingerprints of Johannes Zuch are all over it. Johannes Zuch, Jonathan Blow - see how they braided them together? (Sorry).

Whilst this has been created by Rockstar as a pastiche - as much loving send-up as it is withering take down - and designed to make a quick joke in the early 'Feng Shui' mission, the game is playable from start to finish if you so desire. You boot it up by inserting a physical disc, too, which is funny given the context. And it's good! Well, not good good, but it's a proper brainteaser, and ribs 2016's The Witness with such knowledge and (I think?) respect that it's hard not to be charmed by Rockstar's game-within-a-game. There are collectibles to be found that riff on Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves, too, a knowing nod to the most try-hard of all try-hard literature.

Recent findings suggest that within seconds of the title screen, too, you're presented with a game-within-a-game-within-a-game. You must clear four boards filled with puzzle pieces as the protagonist mutters something mysterious and weird in his posh voice. Do so, and you unlock the door to the next location. Head up to a bunker, and you'll see a room filled with various clues - maybe it's a flashing lamp flickering in morse code, maybe it's a malfunctioning clock presenting a maths puzzle, maybe it's a pricetag on a record that changes on every visit, maybe it's a photograph with anomalous elements, maybe it's a "Developed Using Zuchworks Engine" easter egg hidden in the environment. You need to keep your wits about you, because one of these clues changes every time you enter - and the clue corresponds to a date that changes on a calendar on the wall.

You can look up a guide if you need to, or you can spend far too long figuring out how all this relates to the telephone you can find in the room on your own, like muggins here, before opening up the path to the next puzzle. Look at the image below to see the level of record-keeping and brainteasing this bizarre little game prompted from me. I will say, the sense of achievement you get from playing around with this stuff is pretty remarkable, given - let's not forget I'm actually playing Grand Theft Auto 6 whilst I'm wandering around in the black and white murk trying to complete a puzzle game for no actual reward.

In a recent development, the bunker room is, by far, the hardest part of Tenebrae Lux. From here, things ease up: you need to figure out the right sequence of glyphs on a bridge, and then put some distance between yourself and a curious and rather creepy suited man that's seemingly figuring things out ahead of you in a location inspired by, I think, The Backrooms (or Portal, or Superliminal, or maybe something else entirely. Who knows what Zuch was thinking?).

"With the last enigma finally mastered," the narrator drones in his bumbling monotone, "I step forward into the void, the shadows swallow, consuming all, and then finally the sweet embrace of darkness of which there is no end." 'You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience', Tenebrae Lux tells me, before cutting to the best joke of the whole thing: the credits roll much akin to something Hideo Kojima would produce.

Sources indicate that so, what do you get out of all of this? Well - just like real puzzle games in the real world - nothing, really. If you've not completed one of the other three fully playable games in GTA 6, you will get a trophy/achievement. But given the main game is all about Jason and Lucia's desperate scramble to escape the poverty trap, to try and break free of the cycle of debt, violence, and consequence that keeps them clinging to Leonida's seedy underbelly, there's no monetary reward. There's no 'progress' in the sense of the protagonist's shared story.

Industry observers note that even in terms of your own cold, hard, mathematical 'completion' you only need to boot each of the four games up once in order to work towards GTA 6's 100% completion. So what's the point of all this? Why did I spend the better part of 90 minutes trying to figure out how to find a sliver of light in the dark in Tenebrae Lux? The game is a wonderful pastiche in that, essentially, it's not really saying anything. You can probably project some vague meaning onto it if you wish - I'm pretty certain the protagonist literally 'finds himself' at the end - but glib little readings like that are ten-a-penny in this genre.

I think the most impressive thing about Tenebrae Lux is that it exists. You're teased with it in an early mission - Rockstar may as well say 'look, we put a game in a game, lol' - but it's more than that. This is what happens when Rockstar's 4700-plus developers are given the room to… develop. Tenebrae Lux could very easily have been a non-interactive experience, a quick, cheap joke shown over-the-shoulder taking a drive-by pop shot at Johnathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck, or any and all of the above. Or maybe it could be a 'vertical slice', an incomplete demo, a teaser. But it's not, because nothing about GTA 6 is quick or cheap.

GTA 6, in every single conceivable way, is a premium experience - part-sandbox, part-simulation, part-otherworld. To create not just one, but four fully playable and completable games within that framework is showboating, sure, but to make that game actually good and - perhaps controversially - even better than some of the games it's pastiching… Well, it's just rubbing salt in the wound, really.

A code for the game was provided by Cal Hampton.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are?
  • Industry observers note that right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea.
  • Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the new game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

Industry observers note that right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their new life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

Recent findings suggest that until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

"Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community.".

Here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

In a recent development, it's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It shows us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

According to recent reports, it may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the broader markets are seeing red today, primarily led lower by yet another steep selloff in technology and artificial intelligence stocks.
  • Recent findings suggest that this morning, the discount retail chain Dollar Tree, Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The broader markets are seeing red today, primarily led lower by yet another steep selloff in technology and artificial intelligence stocks. But one manufacturer nearly as far from those sectors as you can get is seeing its share price surge by over 10% today: the discount retailer Dollar Tree. Here’s what you need to know. What’s happened? This morning, the discount retail chain Dollar Tree, Inc. (Nasdaq: DLTR) reported its third-quarter fiscal 2026 results, which cover the three-month period ending October 31. The most salient metrics from those results are as follows: Net sales: $5.1 billion Adjusted earnings per share (EPS): $1.16 Comparable store net sales: up 4.6% Foot traffic increase: 3.8% New stores: 84 Total stores: 9,511 To put those financials in perspective, LSEG analysts estimated $5.04 billion in net sales and earnings per share of 91 cents, notes Reuters. Announcing the company’s Q3 results, Dollar Tree CEO Mike Creedon said, “Our third quarter results show the strength of Dollar Tree’s value proposition and the progress we’ve made to improve the customer experience. Comp traffic accelerated to 3.8% and drove comparable sales above the high end of our outlook. Our broader assortment, better stores and stronger customer engagement give shoppers more reasons to choose Dollar Tree and come back more often.” Why are Dollar Tree’s shares surging? After announcing its Q3, DLTR stock surged—one of the few to do so today on Wall Street. Dollar Tree’s price jump comes down to a few factors, both of which seem to have pleased investors, based on the company’s share price. The first was the net sales and earnings per share beat. Net sales increased by 6.9% versus the same quarter a year earlier. This was helped by a 4.6% increase in comparable net store sales. Those comps were driven by a 3.8% increase in foot traffic and a 0.8% increase in the amount people spend on an average ticket. In other words, most of the comp increase was not driven by higher tickets, but by increased foot traffic—which is exactly what you want as you enter the final quarter of the year: the all-key holiday period. In addition to favorable quarterly results, another factor that buoyed investors’ view of the company was its full-year fiscal 2026 outlook. Dollar Tree increased its full-year earnings per share range to between $8.05 and $8.25. That was up from its prior range of $7.70 to $8.05. DLTR’s up more than 60% in six months As of the time of this writing, DLTR shares are right now trading up 11% to $154.41 on the back of its Q3 results. That’s an exceptional one-day jump for a discount retailer, but it goes to show the faith investors currently have in the company, which may be one of the few to benefit from an inflation-wary consumer. As prices rise, people tend to cut back on discretionary spending, which can cause downward pressure on retailer shares. But as everyday costs get higher, consumers also tend to shop around for the best price for essentials and everyday items. Dollar Tree has a low-cost pricing structure (many items cost around $1.25, with higher-priced items selling for between $3 and $7) that appeals to cash-strapped consumers operating in an economy where sticker prices at higher-end retailers seem increasingly out of reach. While the company’s roughly 11% share price jump today (as of the time of this writing) is impressive, looking back a little further reveals even better stock price growth. In the past month alone, DLTR shares are up 22%, and over the past six months, DLTR shares are up 61%.

Industry observers note that sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

In a recent development, the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

According to recent reports, there's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

In a recent development, use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Industry observers note that most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Recent findings suggest that also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Recent findings suggest that don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF reveals what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Sources indicate that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

According to recent reports, across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

94% of the world’s biggest songs have one surprising thing in common

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while there is still no recipe for becoming a globally recognized musician, there is one thing that is consistently getting artists on the charts: TikTok.
  • While there is still no recipe for becoming a globally recognized musician, there is one thing that is consistently getting artists on the charts: TikTok.
  • According to recent reports, tikTok’s recent 2026 Music Impact Report found that 94% of songs that entered the Billboard top 200 chart this year went viral on TikTok first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while there is still no recipe for becoming a globally recognized musician, there is one thing that is consistently getting artists on the charts: TikTok. TikTok’s recent 2026 Music Impact Report found that 94% of songs that entered the Billboard top 200 chart this year went viral on TikTok first. The link is stronger than before: in 2024, TikTok found that 84% of songs on the charts had gone viral on the platform first,  up ten percentage points in two years. TikTok virality also affects how long a song stays on the chart. The report also found that tracks that went viral on the platform stayed on the charts for four times longer than those that didn’t catch a moment of popularity on the platform. For instance, songs that had a viral moment on TikTok would spend eight weeks on Billboard charts, as opposed to just two weeks for non-viral hits. But the charts are not the only metric artists use to measure their success and growth, their performance on streaming platforms matters too. The report also found that TikTok virality influences streaming, with 74% of the fastest-growing artists on streaming platforms saw their streams rise alongside their views on TikTok. Sienna Spiro is among the breakthrough artists who rose to fame through the platform, starting her career singing songs to a small audience on TikTok, eventually landing on the VMA stage this year singing her hit song Great Expectations. While a relatively small artist just a year ago, she found a viral moment in her song Die on This Hill, with millions of fans using the sound for their TikToks, giving her recognition beyond the platform. Additionally, the platform’s fresh “add to music app” feature, which lets users connect their TikTok to their streaming service to automatically save songs from videos to their playlists, contributed to Spiro’s streaming success. According to the report, millions of users used the feature to save the single to their music apps. Spiro’s viral hit led her to enter the top 20 of the Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for 13 weeks.

#116496. Breaking: Has Rockstar taken the "Grand Theft Auto" out of GTA 6? Or has it just gamified car-jacking properly for the first time?

Breaking: Has Rockstar taken the "Grand Theft Auto" out of GTA 6? Or has it just gamified car-jacking properly for the first time?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's impossible to have a big game launch these days without some section of the internet, somewhere, finding grievances with the final product because it does not align with the expectations they had pre-release.
  • Industry observers note that the most recent upset comes in the form of Grand Theft Auto 6's revised take on, well, grand theft auto.
  • Industry observers note that so it makes sense that the internet is in a bit of a spin about GTA 6's more mature and restrained take on its eponymous crime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's impossible to have a big game launch these days without some section of the internet, somewhere, finding grievances with the final product because it does not align with the expectations they had pre-release.

Industry observers note that the most recent upset comes in the form of Grand Theft Auto 6's revised take on, well, grand theft auto. In case you're one of the few still unfamiliar, grand theft auto is more than the titular moniker for Rockstar's premier crime simulation series; it's actually a US legal term for the act of stealing or attempting to steal a motor vehicle. In most previous GTA entries, this was a central part of the core gameplay loop: accept a mission, nick a car, complete the mission, nick another car, getaway. It's an endemic part of the loop, and has become so popular and identifiable as such that even other games - Watch Dogs, Saint's Row, Cyberpunk 2077, and so on - have emulated the mechanic.

Industry observers note that so it makes sense that the internet is in a bit of a spin about GTA 6's more mature and restrained take on its eponymous crime. A quick, no-frills getaway in a vehicle you've hijacked on the road isn't always the most effective option. A mindless crime spree on the streets of Leonida is not a simple thing to pull off, nor an easy thing to live down. In this game, actions have consequences, and an ill-timed or ill-judged car jacking can rapidly and efficiently put an end to your criminal ambitions.

According to recent reports, that's not to say you cannot simply steal cars. Of course you can: the option to saunter up to an occupied vehicle and jack it from its registered owner is available to you from the very beginning of the game. But the citizens of Leonida aren't going to take your wanton act of foolishness lying down; many of the motorists in the county will fight back, pull a piece on you, or run you over mid-robbery attempt. Even if you are lucky to find one of the more pliant residents of the city, you might find something peculiar is happening in their car. I jacked a woman in the city over the weekend, and the cat she was ferrying from place to place decided to attack me, causing me to crash. I've heard other people say they've had muffled cries coming from the boot of the car where someone is transporting a hostage, or incidents where they've jacked the same person multiple times, leading to the poor car's owner to have a breakdown in the middle of the city.

It has been revealed that that cat event, the team here at Eurogamer has worked out, is an early game trigger - it seems stealing random cars early in the game will increase the chance of this encounter occurring. Rockstar's guiding hand is more visible here, then, in trying to teach you a lesson: don't steal cars. You're given your own - Jason's two-door coupé utility, a Vapid Creado - that I actually formed quite an emotional bond with in the opening 10-or-so hours of the game. 'Look after this car,' Rockstar insists, tutorialising you how to repair it, customise it, make it all pretty so it's in good condition when you go pick up Lucia for the first time.

Sources indicate that shortly after the 10 hour marker, narrative events whisk you away elsewhere and you're given a 'slim jim', a long, thin tool that allows you to break into locked cars - something you could only do with a quick elbow jab before. The benefit here is two-fold; you can break into cars without setting off their alarms, and without breaking glass and lowering their resale value (something quite important in the earlier sections of the game). So, it takes you until Chapter 2 to start being able to more reliably and consistently break into vehicles. Good.

In a recent development, and it'll take even longer to break into keyless vehicles. We're in 2026 after all, and it's heavily implied this is when GTA 6 is also set - it stands to reason that many cars run keyless fobs, and your old-school tools won't cut it if you want to break into a Zorruso, rather than an old Vapid truck. But then, even when you're well-armed and ready to start an illustrious new career as Vice City's most nefarious car thief, there's more to consider. Most modern cars also come with trackers: standard trackers simply prevent you modding cars you don't own (not an glitch you'll face very often), but advanced trackers are more problematic.

Boosting a car with an advanced tracker immediately alerts the cops to your location, and they close in on you fast. The only answer to this problem is flooring it, and outspeeding the signal ping the tracker is sending out: you need to drive fast and cleanly in order to stay mobile long enough for the tracker to deactivate, and this often incurs damage that makes selling these cars to fences a less viable option. You can't even sell cars with trackers installed at all to some fences until you're much, much further into the game.

Industry observers note that so, long story short, stealing cars is a faff in GTA 6. But I like that. I like that Rockstar has evolved the gameplay formula to more accurately reflect the state of the world in 2026. Modern problems require modern answers, and given that Rockstar has gone above and beyond in its creation of a sandbox simulation of Florida, I feel the immersion would be broken by just being able to saunter up to any car you want and break into it. No, needing a 'slim jim' or a key cloner - or needing to case my victims properly before trying to jack them - makes for a better game as far as I'm concerned. It makes me roleplay Jason and Lucia better, it makes me engage with the game's systems more, it makes me appreciate the cars that I do have whilst I have them.

It has been revealed that it also improves the flow of the game and how I interact with missions. I recently played GTA: Vice City, and after most missions were wrapped up, I would simply fling the nearest motorist onto the sidewalk, hop in their car, and drive away into the Malibu-styled sunset. I can't simply do that in GTA 6: I need to think about my getaway options, whether there's heat on my car, and where my next best (and cheapest) ride is going to be if a robbery or raid goes awry. 'Ah,' I think, 'I understand why there's a garage next to that safehouse on the map now.'.

In making the act of grand theft auto harder and more awkward, Rockstar has nudged me into playing Grand Theft Auto the game like a more thoughtful criminal. I play it like someone on the run, who wouldn't just be indiscriminately committing wanton acts of felony theft on a whim, just because I didn't want to run four blocks down the road to meet my pals for a drink. It's a gorgeous example of functionality, design, and narrative dovetailing - one of the key reasons this is a five star game. The complaints about the system, to my ear, don't reflect what Rockstar has built here. Plus, if it bothers you that much, you could always try to play GTA 6 like a mindless thug if you really want to - just expect the world to treat you like one, too.

Why your HSA needs a succession plan

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.But HSAs have their limits.
  • Health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.But HSAs have their limits.
  • Recent findings suggest that whereas tax-sheltered retirement account owners will pay taxes on the dollars they put into a retirement account (Roth) or on their withdrawals (traditional tax-deferred), HSAs are a unicorn account type—the funds are tax-free every step of the way, provided you spend the money on qualified healthcare expenses.Those tax benefits are magnified for people who pay their healthcare expenses out of pocket, invest in long-term investment assets, and are in higher tax brackets.Given those prodigious tax benefits, an HSA investor would have a bigger balance than a person investing in an IRA, 401(k), or taxable brokerage account, assuming the same contribution amounts, rates of return, tax rates, and holding periods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.But HSAs have their limits. The HSA’s tax benefits effectively cease upon the account owner’s death, or the death of his or her spouse if that person is the beneficiary.That makes it crucial to have a succession plan for your HSA: a plan to encourage tax-free spending during your lifetime (and your spouse’s, if you have one), as well as naming the correct beneficiary for the account to maximize the tax benefits. HSAs give during your lifetime . . . Whereas tax-sheltered retirement account owners will pay taxes on the dollars they put into a retirement account (Roth) or on their withdrawals (traditional tax-deferred), HSAs are a unicorn account type—the funds are tax-free every step of the way, provided you spend the money on qualified healthcare expenses.Those tax benefits are magnified for people who pay their healthcare expenses out of pocket, invest in long-term investment assets, and are in higher tax brackets.Given those prodigious tax benefits, an HSA investor would have a bigger balance than a person investing in an IRA, 401(k), or taxable brokerage account, assuming the same contribution amounts, rates of return, tax rates, and holding periods. That’s because investors in those other account types pay taxes along the way: at time of contribution (Roth), during accumulation (taxable), and/or at time of withdrawal (taxable, traditional tax-deferred). . . . And take after death If your spouse is the designated beneficiary of your HSA, the HSA becomes theirs after your death, and the tax benefits continue. They can continue to take tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenses.But if a person other than your spouse inherits the HSA, the account becomes less attractive than the other key account types mentioned before. An HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary effectively ceases to be an HSA upon the account owner’s death, and all of its tax benefits go away at that time. Moreover, the nonspouse beneficiary will need to include the inherited HSA amount in their income and pay taxes on it.The tax treatment of an HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary is a bit worse than the tax treatment of other major account types that nonspouse beneficiaries might inherit. Heirs enjoy tax-free withdrawals on inherited Roth accounts. Traditional IRA beneficiaries owe taxes, but they at least enjoy some flexibility on the timing of their withdrawals and tax bills. Heirs inheriting taxable accounts have it even better, in that their cost basis becomes whatever the account holdings’ values were on the date of your death. You need a plan for handling your HSA That meh tax treatment on HSAs inherited by nonspouse beneficiaries highlights the value of having a plan to maximize your HSA’s long-term tax benefits. Step 1: Get a system for spending from it Spending from the HSA during your and your spouse’s lifetimes is key, so every HSA owner needs a spending plan. That’s true whether you’re paying healthcare expenses as you incur them or investing the funds for retirement.If you’ve been paying your healthcare costs out of pocket in an effort to allow your account to grow, you can later use the HSA for non-healthcare expenses, provided you have receipts to substantiate those previous out-of-pocket healthcare costs. Ideally, you’d scan and document those expenditures as you incur them. If you’re a married person who’s overseeing your household’s HSA, make sure your spouse understands the withdrawal rules, where to find receipts, and how to submit them to the HSA provider. Step 2: Assign the correct beneficiaries Next, give care to naming beneficiaries. If you’re married, your spouse is a sensible beneficiary for the HSA; as noted earlier, they will be able to take over ownership of the account after your death and keep its full tax benefits during their lifetime.Nonspouse beneficiaries won’t receive the same favorable tax treatment. However, if you think a nonspouse beneficiary still will benefit from the money, that’s probably a good enough reason to leave them the HSA. But other accounts should take precedence.A charity can also make an excellent HSA beneficiary, as the charity won’t need to pay taxes on that amount. That strategy can be particularly appropriate for single people who are charitably inclined, or for surviving spouses. If you’re married, consider making your spouse the primary beneficiary and a charity the secondary. Step 3: Make sure your beneficiaries understand the rules about HSAs If your spouse will inherit your HSA, be sure to underscore the value of liquidating the account during his or her lifetime.While it’s generally not advisable for a nonspouse beneficiary to inherit an HSA, if that’s your plan, it’s important to let your loved ones know that they can reduce the taxable amount in the HSA by paying any of your unpaid medical bills from the HSA. They just need to pay those bills out of your HSA within a year of your death. This article was provided to The Associated Press by Morningstar.
